title: Reading Numbers
description: Reading Numbers — Reading numbers of 2 or more digits · Reading numbers that tell time · Reading numbers that show scales or ratios, and more

blocks.heading: Reading Numbers
blocks.lead: Guidelines set by the Office of the Royal Society — 12 topics

sections.heading: Reading numbers of 2 or more digits
sections.html:
If the last digit is 1, pronounce it “เอ็ด” (et), for example:

WrittenRead as

11

สิบ-เอ็ด (sip-et)

21

ยี่-สิบ-เอ็ด (yi-sip-et)

101

ร้อย-เอ็ด, หฺนึ่ง-ร้อย-เอ็ด (roi-et, nueng-roi-et)

1001

พัน-เอ็ด, หฺนึ่ง-พัน-เอ็ด (phan-et, nueng-phan-et)

2501

สอง-พัน-ห้า-ร้อย-เอ็ด (song-phan-ha-roi-et)

56,000,000,000,001

ห้า-สิบ-หก-ล้าน-ล้าน-เอ็ด (ha-sip-hok-lan-lan-et)

For numbers of 8 or more digits where the millions digit is 1, read it as "เอ็ด" (et), for example:

WrittenRead as
501,741,222ห้า-ร้อย-เอ็ด-ล้าน-เจ็ด-แสน-สี่-หฺมื่น-หฺนึ่ง-พัน-สอง-ร้อย-ยี่-สิบ-สอง (ha-roi-et-lan-chet-saen-si-muen-nueng-phan-song-roi-yi-sip-song)
94,567,501,654,306เก้า-สิบ-สี่-ล้าน-ห้า-แสน-หก- (kao-sip-si-lan-ha-saen-hok-)
หฺมื่น-เจ็ด-พัน-ห้า-ร้อย-เอ็ด-ล้าน-หก-แสน-ห้า-หฺมื่น-สี่-พัน-สาม-ร้อย-หก (muen-chet-phan-ha-roi-et-lan-hok-saen-ha-muen-si-phan-sam-roi-hok)

Source: How to Read and How to Write (อ่านอย่างไร และ เขียนอย่างไร), Royal Institute edition
23rd printing, June 2018, pp. 71–72

sections.heading: Reading Numbers That Tell the Time
sections.html:
Reading Numbers That Tell the Time

Reading hours with no minutes, for example:

Written

Read as

05.00 hrs or 05:00 hrsห้า-นา-ลิ-กา (ha-na-li-ka)
24.00 hrs or 24:00 hrsยี่-สิบ-สี่-นา-ลิ-กา (yi-sip-si-na-li-ka)
00.00 hrs or 00:00 hrsสูน-นา-ลิ-กา (sun-na-li-ka)
Reading hours and minutes, for example:
Written
Read as
11.35 hrs or 11:35 hrs
สิบ-เอ็ด-นา-ลิ-กา-สาม-สิบ-ห้า-นา-ที (sip-et-na-li-ka-sam-sip-ha-na-thi)
16.30 hrs or 16:30 hrs
สิบ-หก-นา-ลิ-กา-สาม-สิบ-นา-ที (sip-hok-na-li-ka-sam-sip-na-thi)
00.05 hrs or 00:05 hrs
สูน-นา-ลิ-กา-ห้า-นา-ที (sun-na-li-ka-ha-na-thi)

Reading hours, minutes and seconds, for example:

Written

Read as

7:30:45เจ็ด-นา-ลิ-กา-สาม-สิบ-นา-ที-สี่-สิบ-ห้า-วิ-นา-ที (chet-na-li-ka-sam-sip-na-thi-si-sip-ha-wi-na-thi)
02:28:15สอง-นา-ลิ-กา-ยี่-สิบ-แปด-นา-ที-สิบ-ห้า-วิ-นา-ที (song-na-li-ka-yi-sip-paet-na-thi-sip-ha-wi-na-thi)
Reading times with fractions of a second: the digits after the decimal point, being fractions of a second, are read one by one, for example:

Written

Read as

8:02:37.86แปด-นา-ลิ-กา-สอง-นา-ที-สาม-สิบ-เจ็ด-จุด-แปด-หก-วิ-นา-ที (paet-na-li-ka-song-na-thi-sam-sip-chet-chut-paet-hok-wi-na-thi)
10-14-24.37สิบ-นา-ลิ-กา-สิบ-สี่-นา-ที-ยี่-สิบ-สี่-จุด-สาม-เจ็ด-วิ-นา-ที (sip-na-li-ka-sip-si-na-thi-yi-sip-si-chut-sam-chet-wi-na-thi)
Note
Writing times with a colon ( : ) between the hours, minutes and seconds is the general practice, while using a hyphen ( - ) between the hours, minutes and seconds is the style used in navigation and astronomy.


Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing, June 2018, pp. 73–75

sections.heading: Reading Numbers That Express Scales or Ratios
sections.html:
For example
Written
Read as
1:100,000
หฺนึ่ง-ต่อ-แสน หรือ หฺนึ่ง-ต่อ-หฺนึ่ง-แสน (nueng-to-saen or nueng-to-nueng-saen)
1:2:4
หฺนึ่ง-ต่อ-สอง-ต่อ-สี่ (nueng-to-song-to-si)

Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing, June 2018, p. 75

sections.heading: Reading Numbers with a Point
sections.html:
1. For numbers with a decimal point, read the digits before the decimal point as a cardinal number and the digits after the decimal point one by one, for example:

Written

Read as

1.235หฺนึ่ง-จุด-สอง-สาม-ห้า (nueng-chut-song-sam-ha)
51.08ห้า-สิบ-เอ็ด-จุด-สูน-แปด (ha-sip-et-chut-sun-paet)


Numbers expressing money or units of measurement are read according to that currency or unit, for example:

Written

Read as

5.80 baht

ห้า-บาด-แปด-สิบ-สะ-ตาง (ha-bat-paet-sip-sa-tang)
8.65 dollarsแปด-ดอน-ล่า-หก-สิบ-ห้า-เซ็น (paet-don-la-hok-sip-ha-sen)
3.58 metersสาม-เมด-ห้า-สิบ-แปด-เซ็น-ติ-เมด (sam-met-ha-sip-paet-sen-ti-met)
2.205 kilogramsสอง-กิ-โล-กฺรำ- สอง-ร้อย- ห้า-กฺรำ (song-ki-lo-kram-song-roi-ha-kram)

2. For numbers with a dot that indicate order, read the digits after the dot as cardinal numbers

WrittenRead as
3.11สาม-จุด-สิบ-เอ็ด (sam-chut-sip-et)
10.17สิบ-จุด-สิบ-เจ็ด (sip-chut-sip-chet)

Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing, June 2018, pp. 72–73

sections.heading: Reading House Numbers
sections.html:
House numbers with a slash (/) and those without follow the same reading rules: house numbers with 2 digits are read as whole numbers; those with 3 or more digits may be read either digit by digit or as whole numbers; digits after the slash (/) are read digit by digit, for example:

House number 10 is read บ้าน-เลก-ที่ สิบ (ban-lek-thi sip)

House number 414 is read บ้าน-เลก-ที่ สี่-หฺนึ่ง-สี่ (ban-lek-thi si-nueng-si)

or บ้าน-เลก-ที่ สี่-ร้อย-สิบ-สี่ (ban-lek-thi si-roi-sip-si). House number 56/342 is read บ้าน-เลก-ที่ ห้า-สิบ-หก ทับ สาม-สี่-สอง (ban-lek-thi ha-sip-hok thap sam-si-song). House number 657/21 is read บ้าน-เลก-ที่ หก-ห้า-เจ็ด ทับ สอง-หฺนึ่ง (ban-lek-thi hok-ha-chet thap song-nueng) or บ้าน-เลก-ที่ หก-ร้อย-ห้า-สิบ-เจ็ด ทับ-สอง- หฺนึ่ง (ban-lek-thi hok-roi-ha-sip-chet thap-song-nueng)

Groups of digits beginning with 0 are always read digit by digit, for example:

House number 0864/1108 is read บ้าน-เลก-ที่ สูน-แปด-หก-สี่-ทับ-หฺนึ่ง-หฺนึ่ง-สูน-แปด (ban-lek-thi sun-paet-hok-si-thap-nueng-nueng-sun-paet)

Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing, June 2018, pp. 76–77

sections.heading: Reading Postal Codes
sections.html:
A postal code is a group of digits designed to indicate the destination of postal items and to represent area details, so that postal items can be sorted and forwarded to their destination accurately and quickly. A postal code consists of 5 digits: the first 2 digits indicate the province and the last 3 digits indicate the post office of that province. For example, in postal code 32190, 32 indicates Surin Province and 190 indicates the Surin post and telegraph office responsible for delivering postal items in Chumphon Buri District, Surin Province


Postal codes are read digit by digit, as follows:
Postal code 32190 is read ระ-หัด-ไปฺร-สะ-นี สาม-สอง-หฺนึ่ง-เก้า-สูน (ra-hat-prai-sa-ni sam-song-nueng-kao-sun)

Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing
June 2018, p. 77

sections.heading: Reading Highway Numbers
sections.html:
In the past, major highways were usually named after the surname of an important person connected with the route, such as its pioneer or builder. As more roads were built, using surnames became cumbersome and confusing, and it was impossible to tell which region of the country a route was in. A numbering system was therefore introduced for highways under the care of the Department of Highways — national highways, concession highways and motorways — according to the following rules:

11.1 Single-digit highways are national highways and motorways that serve as main routes linking region to region, namely:
– National Highway No. 1, or Phahonyothin Road, is the main road to the Northern Region, starting in Bangkok and ending in Chiang Rai Province
– National Highway No. 2, or Mittraphap Road, is the main road to the Northeastern Region, starting in Saraburi Province and ending in Nong Khai Province
– National Highway No. 3, or Sukhumvit Road, is the main road to the central provinces and the southeastern coast, starting in Bangkok and ending in Trat Province
– National Highway No. 4, or Phetkasem Road, is the main road to the Southern Region, starting in Bangkok and ending in Sadao District, Songkhla Province
– Motorway No. 5 links the Bangkok Outer Ring Road to Chiang Rai Province
– Motorway No. 6 links the Bangkok Outer Ring Road to Nong Khai Province
– Motorway No. 7 links the Bangkok Outer Ring Road to Chanthaburi Province
– Motorway No. 8 links the Bangkok Outer Ring Road to Padang Besar Railway Station, Sadao District, Songkhla Province
– Motorway No. 9 is the Bangkok Outer Ring Road

11.2 Two-digit highways are national highways or motorways that are main routes within each region. For example, National Highway No. 22 is the main national highway in the Northeastern Region, Udon Thani–Nakhon Phanom route; Motorway No. 51 is the highway linking the Bangkok Outer Ring Road to Suphan Buri

11.3 Three-digit highways are secondary national highways. For example, National Highway No. 202 is a secondary national highway in the Northeastern Region, Chaiyaphum–Khemarat route; National Highway No. 314 is a secondary national highway in the Central Region, Bang Pakong–Chachoengsao route

11.4 Four-digit highways are national highways linking a province with its districts or important places in that province. For example, Highway No. 4006 is a highway in the Southern Region branching off Highway No. 4 (Ratchakrut–Lang Suan)

Highway numbers are read digit by digit, as follows:

Highway No. 21

Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-ทาง-หฺลวง สอง-หฺนึ่ง (mai-lek-thang-luang song-nueng)
Highway No. 314
Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-ทาง-หฺลวง สาม-หฺนึ่ง-สี่ (mai-lek-thang-luang sam-nueng-si)

Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing
June 2018, pp. 83–85

sections.heading: Reading Telephone Numbers
sections.html:
Telephone numbers are read digit by digit. Originally, the number 2 was read as โท (tho) so that the sounds of “2” and “3” would be distinct, since telephone numbers consist of many digits and sometimes several 2s and 3s appear in sequence, and the sounds of "2" and "3" are similar. Later, as telephone systems improved greatly and “2” was no longer confused with "3", the digit "2" in telephone numbers came to be read as สอง (song), for example: 0 2225 8622 is read สูน สอง-สอง-สอง-ห้า แปด-หก-สอง-สอง (sun song-song-song-ha paet-hok-song-song)


1. Domestic telephone numbers


In 2001, a format for domestic telephone numbers, both landline and mobile, was introduced by merging the existing long-distance codes or mobile codes into the telephone number to form a 9-digit number. The writing and reading of telephone numbers, which previously read the long-distance code or mobile code first and then the telephone number, has been changed* as follows:


In Bangkok and its vicinity, which previously had the long-distance code 02, write as follows:


Telephone number 0 2531 3234


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ สูน-สอง-ห้า-สาม-หฺนึ่ง สาม-สอง-สาม-สี่ (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap sun-song-ha-sam-nueng sam-song-sam-si)


Telephone number 0 2643 5151-2


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ สูน-สอง-หก-สี่-สาม ห้า-หฺนึ่ง-ห้า-หฺนึ่ง ถึง สอง (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap sun-song-hok-si-sam ha-nueng-ha-nueng thueng song)


Telephone number 0 2356 0466-70 ext. 2002


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ สูน สอง-สาม-ห้า-หก สูน-สี่-หก-หก ถึง เจ็ด-สูน ต่อ สอง-สูน-สูน-สอง (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap sun song-sam-ha-hok sun-si-hok-hok thueng chet-sun to song-sun-sun-song)


In other provinces, such as Phetchaburi Province, which previously had the long-distance code 032, write as follows:


Telephone number 0 3221 1234


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ สูน สาม-สอง-สอง-หฺนึ่ง หฺนึ่ง-สอง-สาม-สี่ (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap sun sam-song-song-nueng nueng-song-sam-si)


For mobile phone numbers with prefixes such as 081, 089, 090, write the mobile prefix followed by the phone number, as follows:


Telephone number 08 1553 0743


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ สูน-แปด หฺนึ่ง-ห้า-ห้า-สาม สูน-เจ็ด-สี่-สาม (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap sun-paet nueng-ha-ha-sam sun-chet-si-sam)


Telephone number 09 0965 1862


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ สูน-เก้า สูน-เก้า-หก-ห้า หฺนึ่ง-แปด-หก-สอง (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap sun-kao sun-kao-hok-ha nueng-paet-hok-song)


Other kinds of telephone numbers, for example:


Audiotex telephone services have 10 digits: the first group of 4 digits is the system code, the second group of 3 digits is the business owner's code, and the third group of 3 digits is the service type code. Numbers in this system are written in 3 separate groups and read digit by digit, for example:


Telephone number 1900 111 000


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ หฺนึ่ง-เก้า-สูน-สูน หฺนึ่ง-หฺนึ่ง-หฺนึ่ง สูน-สูน-สูน (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap nueng-kao-sun-sun nueng-nueng-nueng sun-sun-sun)


Telephone information services with operators have 4-digit numbers set by the agency or business itself to be easy to remember. Write all 4 digits as a single group and read them digit by digit, for example:


Telephone number 1213


Read as: หฺมาย-เลก-โท-ระ-สับ หฺนึ่ง-สอง-หฺนึ่ง-สาม (mai-lek-tho-ra-sap nueng-song-nueng-sam)


2. International telephone numbers


An international telephone number consists, in order, of the international access code, the + sign [the international prefix sign], the country code, the city code and the telephone number. When making an international call, however, the + sign is not dialled. International telephone numbers may be written according to the standard of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), for example:


099+618 9367 6157


009 is an international dialing code


61 is the country code for Australia


89 is the city code for Perth


367 6157 is the telephone number


001+825 1645 4525


001 is an international dialing code


82 is the country code for Korea


51 is the city code for Busan


645 4525 is the telephone number


International telephone numbers fall into 2 types, as follows:


2.1 Calling abroad


International dialing codes from Thailand vary by service provider, with rates that differ by provider and time of day, e.g. 001, 007, 009. They are written as follows:


001 + 33 8837 1691


Read as: สูน-สูน-หฺนึ่ง สาม-สาม แปด-แปด-สาม-เจ็ด หนึ่ง-หก-เก้า-หฺนึ่ง (sun-sun-nueng sam-sam paet-paet-sam-chet nueng-hok-kao-nueng)


007 + 9 5122 1881


Read as: สูน-สูน-เจ็ด เก้า ห้า-หฺนึ่ง-สอง-สอง หฺนึ่ง-แปด-แปด-หนึ่ง (sun-sun-chet kao ha-nueng-song-song nueng-paet-paet-nueng)


2.2 Calling in from abroad


Start with the international access code of that country, followed by Thailand's country code 66 and the telephone number, dropping the first 0 of the telephone number, for example:


Calling a number in Bangkok and its vicinity from the United States


011+66 2282 2269


Read as: สูน-หฺนึ่ง-หฺนึ่ง หก-หก สอง-สอง-แปด-สอง สอง-สอง-หก-เก้า (sun-nueng-nueng hok-hok song-song-paet-song song-song-hok-kao)
001 is the international access code from the United States


66 is the country code for Thailand


2282 2269 is telephone number 0 2282 2269 with the first 0 dropped


Calling a number in Songkhla Province from France


00+66 7432 3847


Read as: สูน-สูน หก-หก เจ็ด-สี่-สาม-สอง สาม-แปด-สี่-เจ็ด (sun-sun hok-hok chet-si-sam-song sam-paet-si-chet)


00 is the international access code from France


66 is the country code for Thailand
7432 3847 is telephone number 0 7432 3847 with the first 0 dropped


Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing
June 2018, pp. 79–83

sections.heading: Reading Vehicle Registration Plate Numbers
sections.html:
1. For car license plates registered under the Motor Vehicle Act B.E. 2522 (1979), read the category number and category letter first, then read the digits one by one, followed by the name of the province of registration. For license plates under Ministerial Regulation No. 25 (1996) issued under the Motor Vehicle Act B.E. 2522 (1979), read the category letter first, then the digits one by one, followed by the name of the province of registration, for example:

License plate 5ช-2437 Bangkok
Read as: เลก-ทะ-เบียน-ห้า-ชอ-ช้าง สอง-สี่-สาม-เจ็ด กฺรุง-เทบ-มะ-หา-นะ-คอน (lek-tha-bian-ha-cho-chang song-si-sam-chet krung-thep-ma-ha-na-khon)

License plate ภบ 4107 Bangkok

Read as: เลก-ทะ-เบียน พอ-สำ-เพา-บอ-ใบ-ไม้-สี่-หฺนึ่ง-สูน-เจ็ด กฺรุง-เทบ-มะ-หา-นะ-คอน (lek-tha-bian pho-sam-phao-bo-bai-mai-si-nueng-sun-chet krung-thep-ma-ha-na-khon)

2. For car license plates registered under the Land Transport Act B.E. 2522 (1979), read the vehicle-type code number first, then read the digits one by one, followed by the name and code of the province of registration, for example:

License plate 80-2437 Bangkok 01
Read as: เลก-ทะ-เบียน แปด-สูน สอง-สี่-สาม-เจ็ด-กฺรุง-เทบ-มะ-หา-นะ-คอน-สูน-หฺนึ่ง (lek-tha-bian paet-sun song-si-sam-chet-krung-thep-ma-ha-na-khon-sun-nueng)

Source: How to Read and How to Write (อ่านอย่างไร และ เขียนอย่างไร), Royal Institute edition,
23 June 2018, p. 78

sections.heading: Reading Rattanakosin Era (ร.ศ.) Years Given with Their Buddhist Era (พ.ศ.) Equivalent
sections.html:
e.g. R.S. 112 (1893)

Read as: รัด-ตะ-นะ-โก-สิน-สก ร้อย-สิบ-สอง-ตฺรง-กับ-พุด-ทะ-สัก-กะ- หฺราด สอง- (rat-ta-na-ko-sin-sok roi-sip-song-trong-kap-phut-tha-sak-ka-rat song-)
พัน-สี่-ร้อย-สาม-สิบ-หก (phan-si-roi-sam-sip-hok)

(The words “ตรงกับ” (trong kap, “corresponding to”) are added to make the meaning clearer)

Source: How to Read and How to Write (อ่านอย่างไร และ เขียนอย่างไร), Royal Institute edition,
23 June 2018, p. 76

sections.heading: Reading Official Letter Numbers
sections.html:
These are usually read digit by digit, for example:

Letter No. รภ 0001/102 dated 10 October 2017
Read as: หฺนัง-สือ-ที่ รอ-พอ สูน-สูน-สูน-หฺนึ่ง ทับ หฺนึ่ง-สูน-สอง ลง-วัน-ที่ สิบ ตุ-ลา-คม พุด-ทะ-สัก-กะ-หฺราด สอง-พัน-ห้า-ร้อย-หก-สิบ (nang-sue-thi ro-pho sun-sun-sun-nueng thap nueng-sun-song long-wan-thi sip tu-la-khom phut-tha-sak-ka-rat song-phan-ha-roi-hok-sip)

Letter No. ศธ 0030.01/597 dated 8 Nov 1991
Read as: หฺนัง-สือ-ที่ สอ-ทอ สูน-สูน-สาม-สูน-จุด-สูน- หฺนึ่ง-ทับ ห้า-เก้า-เจ็ด-ลง-วัน-ที่ แปด พฺรึด-สะ-จิ-กา-ยน สอง-พัน-ห้า-ร้อย-สาม-สิบ-สี่ (nang-sue-thi so-tho sun-sun-sam-sun-chut-sun-nueng-thap ha-kao-chet-long-wan-thi paet phruet-sa-chi-ka-yon song-phan-ha-roi-sam-sip-si)

Source: How to Read and How to Write (อ่านอย่างไร และ เขียนอย่างไร), Royal Institute edition,
23 June 2018, pp. 75–76

sections.heading: Writing Dates
sections.html:
1. Writing dates

1.1. If the day or the word “วันที่” (date) is given, the abbreviation “พ.ศ.” (B.E.) must precede the year, for example:

Sunday, 1 July 2012

1 July 2012

1.2. If the day is not given or the word “วันที่” (date) is not used, “พ.ศ.” (B.E.) is not needed before the year
Buddhist Era year, for example:

๑ กรกฎาคม ๒๕๕๕ (1 July 2555)

1.3. When writing an abbreviated date, give only the day number and the abbreviated month name
and the last 2 digits of the B.E. year (an informal form, but specified as a guideline), for example:

๑ ก.ค. ๕๕ (1 Jul. 55)

2. Writing date ranges within the same year

Use the word “ถึง” (thueng, “to”) or a hyphen between the dates. The year may or may not be given
after the starting day and month, for example:

13 April 2012 to 28 December 2012

๑๓ เมษายน ๒๕๕๕-๒๘ ธันวาคม ๒๕๕๕ (13 April 2555-28 December 2555)

13 April to 28 December 2012

๑๓ เมษายน-๒๘ ธันวาคม ๒๕๕๕ (13 April-28 December 2555)

13 April 2012 to 28 December 2012

13 April 2012 – 28 December 2012

13 April to 28 December 2012

13 April – 28 December 2012

13 April to 28 December 2012

13 April – 28 December 2012

3. Writing dates spanning different years

Use the word “ถึง” (thueng, “to”) or a hyphen between the starting date and the ending date, for example:

13 April 2011 to 28 December 2012

๑๓ เมษายน ๒๕๕๔-๒๘ ธันวาคม ๒๕๕๕ (13 April 2554-28 December 2555)

13 April 2011 to 28 December 2012

13 April 2011 – 28 December 2012


Source: How to Read and How to Write, Royal Institute Edition, 23rd printing, June 2018, pp. 140–141
